newsitem.title: SPAIN: SOCCER-HISTORY SUGGESTS A MEDITERRANEAN GOAL-FEAST.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-HISTORY SUGGESTS A MEDITERRANEAN GOAL-FEAST.

text.p: Anybody looking for league goals this weekend in Europe need look no further than the top clash in Spain, which pits Valencia against their Mediterranean rivals, Barcelona.
The fixture between two traditionally attacking sides produces an average of nearly four goals a game and has not ended goalless for nearly 30 years.
Last year, Valencia avenged three consecutive defeats with a 4-1 drubbing which helped kill off Barcelona's championship hopes.

Currently, though, there is an ocean between their respective league standings. While Barcelona are battling out second place with Real Betis and Deportivo Coruna, Valencia lie 20 points further back in 10th spot.
But there is pride at stake as well as league points in a game that attracts an unusually large number of travelling fans.
The Easter holiday weekend is likely to see several thousand Barcelona supporters make the 350 km trip down the coast for this season's clash.
For the home fans, there is the prospect of momentary supremacy over a city which has outshone them both as a port and as a soccer side.

Barcelona, the 1992 European champions, already have four league titles to their name this decade. They face a Cup Winners' Cup semifinal against Fiorentina and look set to end the season with some silverware on the sideboard.

In contrast, Valencia have done little in recent seasons to justify their position as one of Spanish football's 'Big Five' although this year they reached the quarter-finals of the UEFA Cup before being knocked out by German team Schalke.
Valencia's last major trophy was the 1981 European Cup Winners' Cup and their real glory days came in the early 1960s with successive victories in the UEFA Cup's predecessor, the European Fairs Cup.
One of those wins came over Barcelona -- 7-3 on aggregate -- and the last of the club's four league titles was snatched on goal difference from the Catalans in the 1970-71 season.
Valencia slipped to the second division in the mid-1980s, but seemed ready to bounce back with an air of optimism created by the election of chairman Paco Roig three years ago.
Promises of trophies helped him win the vote and the dream nearly came true last season when the side finished second to Atletico Madrid.
But Valencia slumped this season with the defection of goalscorer Predrag Mijatovic to Real Madrid, and, with Roig under fire, coach Luis Aragones became the scapegoat.
Aragones jumped before he was pushed after publicly voicing his disapproval of Roig's "throw-a-peseta-at-it" approach to building a team.
Most fans feel Roig should have spent the money on hang on to Mijatovic instead of embarking on a badly-planned spending spree.
Brazilian striker Romario made a fleeting, but profitable, visit and compatriot Viola also clashed with the club and went home.
With things going wrong on the field, supporters were quick to blame Roig, who is regularly subjected to the 'panolada' -- a traditional Spanish protest when fans wave white handkerchiefs.
It has led to an air of uncertainty and coach Jorge Valdano is one of the likely absentees next season although he said this week that there had been no ultimatum from the board.
One good move came with the signing last month of Argentine midfielder Ariel Ortega.
Ortega was unavailable for the end of the UEFA campaign but he has helped turn around the team's fortunes in the league.
However, the Argentine is away on international duty this weekend and heads up a list of absentees that has left Valdano scraping the barrel for players.
In the circumstances he will be doing well to prevent Barcelona from being the only ones to enjoy the probable goal feast.
